title: AWS CWI Exam Prep in Peoria, IL: 6-Day Course
description: Six-day AWS CWI exam prep for Peoria heavy equipment, haul truck, bridge and plant welding inspectors: Part C code choice, Part B travel and AWS eligibility.
h1: AWS CWI Exam Preparation in Peoria: Six Days for Central Illinois Heavy Equipment, Bridge and Plant Welding Inspectors
html:
Peoria's name has travelled the world on yellow machines. In its July 2026 workforce announcement Caterpillar said it employs more than 17,000 people in Illinois, counting its downtown Peoria offices, and named manufacturing operations in East Peoria, Mapleton, Morton, Pontiac and Decatur. In June 2026 Komatsu opened a new Surface Haulage Headquarters and Customer Experience Center in Peoria, and Komatsu said its largest mining truck, the 400-ton 980E-5SE with electric drive, was built in Peoria. Around those two companies sits a supplier base of fabricators, machine shops and weld shops, and the city's traffic crosses the Illinois River on steel bridges. A great deal of that work comes down to welds that somebody has to check against a drawing and a written standard.

Atlantis NDT offers a six-day course that prepares central Illinois welders, fitters, QC inspectors, weld engineers and NDT technicians for the AWS Certified Welding Inspector (CWI) examination. The American Welding Society runs the examination and grants the certification. Every candidate applies to AWS personally and has to meet its education, work experience and vision requirements on his or her own record. AWS has not approved or endorsed this course, and Atlantis has no access to AWS examination content or anyone's scores. There is no Atlantis classroom in Peoria. You can work through the six days online at your own pace, take them as part of a group at your employer's plant, or book them one-to-one, online or in person at a place agreed when you book. The national CWI exam prep page lays out what each day covers.

What Peoria welds: earthmoving machines, haul trucks and river crossings

Heavy equipment is welded in thick sections. Frames, booms, buckets, dump bodies and axle housings are built from plate that often needs preheat, several passes and close control of fit-up, and the finished welds carry cyclic loads for years in quarries, mines and road jobs. Inspection in that kind of plant is mostly about consistency at volume: confirming fit-up before the arc starts, watching preheat and interpass temperature, gauging fillet size and profile on hundreds of near-identical joints, and noticing when a robot program or a fixture has drifted before a whole batch needs rework.

Mining trucks push the scale further. A truck rated at 400 tons has a frame and dump body far larger than anything a typical structural shop handles, and the Peoria haulage hub lists manufacturing management among its functions. The suppliers that feed equipment builders weld brackets, tanks, guards and subassemblies to the customer's drawings. Many of them are audited by the customer's supplier quality engineers, who expect the shop to show who inspected each weld, when, and against which acceptance criteria. A CWI on staff is one of the simplest ways for a small shop to answer that question with confidence.

Machinery welding is not on the Part C list, so plan around it

Machinery and equipment have their own AWS document. In 2024 AWS issued D14.0/D14.0M, Machinery and Equipment Welding Specification, which combines and replaces D14.1 for cranes and material handling equipment, D14.3 for earthmoving, construction and agricultural equipment, D14.4 for the design of welded joints in machinery and D14.5 for presses. Large equipment builders also publish their own welding standards and call them out on drawings, either instead of a public specification or on top of one.

None of these is a Part C option. The AWS CWI page lists AWS D1.1, API 1104, AWS D1.2, AWS D1.5, AWS D15.1, AWS D17.1, the ASME package of Section IX with B31.1 and B31.3, and an ISO standard. For a candidate whose career is spent around machinery, D1.1 is usually the nearest fit. Its terminology for fillet and groove welds, its prequalified joint details, its preheat tables, its welder qualification rules and its visual acceptance criteria are the ideas equipment specifications are written around. Studying D1.1 for the exam is not a substitute for knowing your plant's own standard, but the habits it trains, such as finding the right table fast and reading acceptance criteria literally, carry straight back to the inspection bench.

The Cedar Street Bridge and other steel over the Illinois River

The Illinois River crossings between Peoria and East Peoria include some old steel. In March 2024 WCBU described the three-phase plan IDOT and East Peoria had started for the Cedar Street Bridge, then 92 years old: work on the East Peoria side first, then the ramps at the Main Street interchange, and finally the main span, where IDOT said steel repairs might be needed. In March 2026 IDOT announced that rehabilitation would resume that April with repairs to the bridge's structural steel and driving surface and the replacement of a finger joint, and at the end of May WCBU reported a full closure expected to last until mid-to-late August 2026. Schedules on old bridges move, so check IDOT for the current status before planning around any of this work.

Repair work on an old span is a different job from shop fabrication of new girders. An inspector on a repair contract may check how new plates are cut and fitted against old members, confirm preheat on steel whose exact chemistry nobody can promise, watch repair welds made in cramped positions and document what turned up once paint and rust were blasted away. The contract specification controls. For welding new bridge steel the governing document is normally AASHTO/AWS D1.5, the Bridge Welding Code, whose Clause 12 covers fracture-critical members. A Peoria candidate who expects to work for a bridge fabricator, or for the inspection consultants a highway agency engages, should give D1.5 serious thought for Part C. Background reading: AWS D1.5 explained.

Which code book a Peoria candidate should open in Part C

Part C is the open-book code application test, between 50 and 65 questions on the book you chose when you applied. The editions in the table are the ones AWS listed on its CWI page in November 2026.

Work in central IllinoisPart C bookWhy it fits
Machine frames, booms, buckets, truck bodies, plant platforms and building steelAWS D1.1, 2020 editionThe listed code closest to machinery specifications, covering preheat, prequalified joints, welder tests and visual acceptance
Bridge fabrication, and repair of river crossings and state route bridgesAWS D1.5, 2020 edition including Clause 12Written for highway bridge steel, fracture-critical members included
Steam, boiler and process piping in power stations and plant utilitiesASME Section IX (2023) with B31.1 and B31.3 (2024)Matches the procedure qualification, welder qualification and piping rules those jobs are run under
Gas transmission and distribution pipeline crews working across IllinoisAPI 1104, 22nd editionThe standard pipeline girth welds are qualified and accepted against
Aluminum guards, enclosures, cabs and trailer partsAWS D1.2, 2014 editionThe listed structural aluminum code

Choose the book you expect to use most over the next few years, not the one a friend found easiest. The exam editions AWS names can lag behind the copies on the shelf at work, and clause and table numbers move between editions, so study the edition on the AWS list. Further reading: AWS D1.1, ASME Section IX and API 1104.

Illinois Central College and the AWS Peoria Section

Illinois Central College, based in East Peoria, offers credit welding programs at three levels. Its Welding Operator certificate is a one-semester, 13-credit introduction to shielded metal arc and gas metal arc welding, taught in a lab with 32 welding booths. Those credits count toward the 29-credit Welding Specialist certificate, whose course list adds gas tungsten arc welding, Welding Blueprint Reading, Weld Testing, weld fabrication with both main processes, maintenance welding and a weld certification preparation and testing course, and further toward the Welding Technology associate degree. The college also hosts a student chapter of the American Welding Society.

Two of those ICC courses line up directly with the CWI. Welding symbols run through Part A, so a candidate who took blueprint reading already has a head start, and the bend, tensile and macro tests taught in weld testing are the background to the qualification questions in Parts B and C.

The AWS Peoria Section sits in District 13. It held its February and April 2026 meetings at Illinois Central College, with demonstrations of submerged arc equipment and of Fronius welding machines. Section meetings are a good way to meet working CWIs before you apply, and after certification, technical programs of this kind are one of the ways inspectors collect professional development hours.

Counting your years: the AWS experience table from a Peoria shop floor

AWS sets a sliding scale between schooling and welding-related work. According to the AWS CWI page, a bachelor's degree or higher in welding engineering or welding technology calls for one year of experience; an associate degree or higher in welding or a related engineering technology, engineering or a physical science, two years; engineering or technical courses applicable to a welding bachelor's degree, three; completed trade or vocational courses, four; a high school diploma or equivalent, five; eighth-grade schooling, nine; and less than that, twelve. AWS decides what counts, and it judges duties rather than job titles. Some Peoria examples, all hypothetical:

  • A production welder at an equipment supplier with a high school diploma and six years of welding to drawings, including checking his own fillet sizes and filling in first-piece inspection sheets. That sits above the five-year line if the supplier confirms the dates and duties.
  • An ICC Welding Specialist graduate with three years on a fabrication line. The trade or vocational line asks for four, assuming AWS accepts the program, so a fourth documented year comes first.
  • A manufacturing engineer with a mechanical engineering degree who has spent two years approving weld fixtures, investigating weld rejections and maintaining welding work instructions. The engineering degree places her on the two-year line.
  • A QC inspector whose employer certified him in VT and MT under a written practice built on ASNT SNT-TC-1A, examining welded frames for four years. Whether those years count as welding-related is AWS's decision, and a clear description of the weld inspection duties helps.

Keep the evidence as you go: employer names and dates, the processes and materials you worked with, the drawings or standards you worked to, and a supervisor who can sign. You must also pass the AWS vision test, recorded on the AWS visual acuity form, and time it so the record is still current when you sit the exam. More detail: CWI requirements and career paths.

Part B means a trip: Chicago, Indianapolis or Milwaukee

Parts A and C are computer-based and taken at a Prometric test center after AWS accepts your application. Part B, the practical, is different. AWS runs it at its seminar locations, usually on the Saturday or Sunday after a three-day Part B seminar held Wednesday to Friday at the same site. Chicago is the only Illinois city on the AWS list of CWI training locations, so a Peoria candidate will usually look at Chicago, Indianapolis or Milwaukee, with Detroit and Cleveland further east. AWS publishes the Part B dates for every site on its seminar and exam schedule.

For US exams that include Part B, AWS wants the application six weeks before the Part B date, and every part needs a score of at least 72 percent. Plan for the drive, a hotel night and the chance of a retake. In Part B you answer 46 questions based on hands-on work with the specimens, tools and documents AWS supplies, including applying a welding procedure specification and its procedure qualification record. Spend practice time measuring fillet legs, convexity, undercut and misalignment until the gauge readings become second nature. The CWI exam cost calculator helps with the travel budget.

Six days around production shifts

Plant QC staff in Peoria often work rotating shifts, with overtime when a new model ramps up. The online format lets you spread the six days of material across days off and quiet evenings, with written answers from the instructor when a symbol, a calculation or a code clause will not make sense. A sensible order is to finish the fundamentals and symbols block before the application goes in, work through the D1.1 or other code book while AWS reviews your paperwork, and leave the timed practice papers for the last stretch before Part A. Engineers and supervisors with a fixed weekday schedule sometimes prefer the one-to-one format, which concentrates the six days on whichever part of the exam worries them most.

Bringing the course into a Peoria plant or supplier

For a manufacturer or supplier preparing several inspectors at once, the corporate format brings the six days into the plant. The group can practise on its own production samples, such as a bracket weld with undercut at the toe, a fillet that runs under size at the start, or a groove weld that was ground flush and now needs a judgement, using the gauges the inspectors carry every shift. The Part C sessions can follow D1.1 while the group discusses where the plant's own welding standard differs from it. Plants often time the course ahead of a model launch, a new customer contract or a supplier audit, so that the credential is in place when the auditor asks. Every person still applies to AWS individually, with a personal vision record and experience evidence.

After the CWI: renewals, recertification and NDT methods

Once certified, you renew with AWS at the three-year and six-year points, and the certification runs for nine years in total. At the nine-year point the options AWS lists include passing Part B again, documenting 80 professional development hours, earning the Certified Radiographic Interpreter credential, an endorsement exam taken before the ninth year, the Senior CWI exams or the nine-year course.

In a heavy equipment town, magnetic particle testing is the natural next method, because surface cracks at weld toes are the defect that cyclic loading tends to produce. NDT certification in the United States is usually issued by the employer under its written practice. Atlantis provides training based on ASNT SNT-TC-1A, including MT Level 2, VT Level 2, UT Level 2 and PT Level 2, and the employer certifies afterward. Local pages: NDT training in Peoria, magnetic particle testing in Peoria, ultrasonic testing in Peoria and Practical NDT simulator access from Peoria. CWI exam prep pages for other Midwest cities: Chicago, St. Louis, Indianapolis and Milwaukee.

How to send a Peoria enquiry

Tell us which format you want, how many people need preparing, the Part C book each one plans to take, and roughly when they hope to sit the exam. For a plant group, add the shifts involved and any weeks to avoid, such as a model changeover or an annual shutdown. If someone's experience looks borderline against the AWS table, describe it and we will point out what to confirm with AWS before applying. Fees for each format are quoted on request, and we reply within one business day.

faq.q: Is there an Atlantis classroom in Peoria?
faq.a: No. There is no Atlantis classroom in Peoria. The six days are taken online at your own pace, at your employer's plant as a group, or one-to-one, online or in person at a location agreed when you book. Atlantis has offices in Houston and Hyderabad.

faq.q: My plant welds to an AWS D14 specification or its own standard. Can I use that for Part C?
faq.a: No. Machinery specifications such as AWS D14.0 and company welding standards are not Part C options. Most machinery inspectors choose AWS D1.1, the listed code closest to the way equipment specifications are written.

faq.q: Where would a Peoria candidate take Part B?
faq.a: At an AWS seminar location. Chicago is the only Illinois city on the AWS list, and Indianapolis and Milwaukee are the other sites most Peoria candidates consider. Part B is usually held on the weekend after a three-day Part B seminar at the same site.

faq.q: Does the ICC Welding Specialist certificate reduce the experience I need?
faq.a: Completed trade or vocational courses put you on the four-year line of the AWS table, provided AWS accepts the program and your work as welding-related. Without that, a high school diploma calls for five years.

faq.q: Is there an AWS section in Peoria?
faq.a: Yes. The AWS Peoria Section, part of District 13, held its February and April 2026 meetings at Illinois Central College. The section page and the section finder on aws.org list upcoming meetings.

faq.q: Which code book suits bridge repair work on the Illinois River crossings?
faq.a: AWS D1.5, the Bridge Welding Code, in the 2020 edition AWS lists, including Clause 12 on fracture-critical members. The contract specification still governs each repair.

faq.q: Can an equipment supplier have the six days delivered for its QC team?
faq.a: Yes. In the corporate format the six days are delivered at the supplier's plant, using its own weld samples and gauges. Each inspector still applies to AWS individually.

faq.q: Has AWS approved or endorsed the Atlantis course?
faq.a: No. AWS has not approved or endorsed it, and Atlantis has no access to AWS examination content or results. AWS administers the examination and issues the certification.

faq.q: How do I ask for a quote from Peoria?
faq.a: Use the enquiry link on this page and give the format, the number of candidates and the Part C book each plans to use. We quote the fee for the chosen format on request and reply within one business day.
